Roughly 20 members of the isolated Indigenous group, including women and children, approached a government outpost in Brazil's northeastern Maranhão state on Monday , marking their first known encounter of this kind in decades, Reuters reports. The group reportedly asked for yams before disappearing back into the forest with their food, according to Survival International . Pay Attention Authored by Ed Dowd via Beyond the Narrative , The clustering of preparedness guidance and system failures is not random. Practical steps and why anxiety is still the wrong strategy... Something has shifted in official messaging. Across Europe, the UK's "Be Ready" campaign is telling households to stock three days of water, food, cash, and a radio. The EU's Preparedness Union Strategy, rolled out last year and reinforced recently, aims for 72 hours of household self-sufficiency. Japan, several Nordic countries, and others have issued or updated similar guidance. In the United States, the Pentagon has directed bases toward greater self-sufficiency, and FEMA is running a nationwide Emergency Alert System test today. These are not brand-new ideas. Civil defense and household preparedness have long been sensible policy. records.title: The Guardian view on the Trump, Xi and Putin meeting: it may be a first, but it’s not progress | Editorial
records.summary: A trilateral gathering is good news for China and Russia, but bad for the US – and its traditional allies “Historic” is a neutral descriptor, not a favourable one. Things can be unprecedented for good reason. Donald Trump’s meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China on Thursday will be the first time that the leaders of the US, China and Russia have gathered for talks as a trio. The trilateral on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is striking, but it is not an achievement. The lack of a clear agenda is telling: the spectacle really is the substance. Mr Trump sees international affairs in terms of spheres of influence. This meeting reinforces the obvious conclusion for the rest of the world – that they don’t get to sit at the table, only to be on the plate. Mr Xi promotes the notion of a multipolar world. Others would be more sympathetic if all three governments were not determinedly undermining multilateralism. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? records.title: The Guardian view on ‘two-tier policing’: tackle the myth, don’t pander to it | Editorial
records.summary: Confidence in the system is being corroded by cynical campaigns and far-right propaganda – that is the challenge to be confronted There are many areas of policy where public opinion diverges from evidence. Voters overestimate rates of crime, for example. Many will be sceptical of politicians who say today’s streets are safer than they used to be, although that is the reality. The challenge is to find methods of persuasion that don’t belittle the experiences of people who are afraid, and don’t like to be told their fears are unfounded. But there is a different challenge that arises when the cause of public concern is a problem that doesn’t really exist. Many people are angry about “ two-tier policing ” in Britain, supposedly characterised by disproportionately severe enforcement against white people and leniency towards minorities. There is no evidence to support a systemic bias of that kind. By contrast, the data suggests an imbalance of fair treatment goes the other way. People of colour are underrepresented in the police, disproportionately targeted with stop-and-search policies and, if arrested, likelier to have force used against them. records.summary: Oscar-nominated director delivers a thoroughly unserious biopic, wasting Christian Bale and Sienna Miller’s talents John Madden was a beloved American original, the burly football coach who segued easily from Super Bowl burnout to television darling to the last name in gaming as the NFL was overtaking baseball as the national pastime. When he wasn’t crashing into family rooms on football Sundays and Thanksgivings to break down the game’s rough complexities into fun-sized morsels, he was pressing flesh with everyday Americans while barnstorming the country in his Madden cruiser – the coach bus he depended on to compensate for his well-documented fear of flying. records.title: BMI was never meant to evaluate an individual’s health | Letter
records.summary: Clinicians should start with the patient in front of them to identify obesity, not rely on a 200-year-old method that was aimed at entire populations, says James Capon Your report on a better way to diagnose obesity is welcome, though it is worth remembering how we came to rely on body mass index (BMI) in the first place ( BMI alternative for identifying obesity ‘could prevent misdiagnosis in millions’, 11 November ). The index was devised in the 1830s by the Belgian statistician Adolphe Quetelet, who wanted to describe the “average man” across whole populations. He never intended it as a verdict on any individual’s health, and it was largely forgotten until 1972, when the American physiologist Ancel Keys, most famous for developing the diet-heart hypothesis, revived it and gave it its current name. Again, it was for population studies. Continue reading...

records.title: Am I Caribbean, or am I a tourist? How art helped me find the answer
records.summary: During my visit to the Fuze Caribbean art fair in the Bahamas, I marvelled at how creators captured the complex nature of Caribbeanness Don’t get The Long Wave delivered to your inbox? Sign up here When I tell people I’m travelling to the Bahamas to report on Fuze Caribbean art fair, no one believes I’m really going for work. There are smirks and jokes about it being a tough life, about drinking from coconuts on the beach. The tourist gaze pervades global perceptions of the Caribbean. This week, I speak to the region’s artists about how they use images to speak back. I have Antiguan and Jamaican heritage, so I’m familiar with the fantasies the Caribbean sparks, which Antiguan-American writer Jamaica Kincaid described as so beautiful that its fluffy white clouds, blue spectral waters and “bottomless” black nights seemed “unreal”. Images have done much to flatten the Caribbean in the global imagination – so why shouldn’t Caribbean people use images to speak back? Continue reading...

Now part of the Mercedes team, Reid Wiseman has been to the moon and with it brings a perspective like no other. records.title: The Guardian view on ‘two-tier policing’: tackle the myth, don’t pander to it | Editorial
records.summary: Confidence in the system is being corroded by cynical campaigns and far-right propaganda – that is the challenge to be confronted There are many areas of policy where public opinion diverges from evidence. Voters overestimate rates of crime, for example. Many will be sceptical of politicians who say today’s streets are safer than they used to be, although that is the reality. The challenge is to find methods of persuasion that don’t belittle the experiences of people who are afraid, and don’t like to be told their fears are unfounded. But there is a different challenge that arises when the cause of public concern is a problem that doesn’t really exist. Many people are angry about “ two-tier policing ” in Britain, supposedly characterised by disproportionately severe enforcement against white people and leniency towards minorities. There is no evidence to support a systemic bias of that kind. By contrast, the data suggests an imbalance of fair treatment goes the other way. People of colour are underrepresented in the police, disproportionately targeted with stop-and-search policies and, if arrested, likelier to have force used against them. records.title: BMI was never meant to evaluate an individual’s health | Letter
records.summary: Clinicians should start with the patient in front of them to identify obesity, not rely on a 200-year-old method that was aimed at entire populations, says James Capon Your report on a better way to diagnose obesity is welcome, though it is worth remembering how we came to rely on body mass index (BMI) in the first place ( BMI alternative for identifying obesity ‘could prevent misdiagnosis in millions’, 11 November ). The index was devised in the 1830s by the Belgian statistician Adolphe Quetelet, who wanted to describe the “average man” across whole populations. He never intended it as a verdict on any individual’s health, and it was largely forgotten until 1972, when the American physiologist Ancel Keys, most famous for developing the diet-heart hypothesis, revived it and gave it its current name. records.title: Twenty years ago, the Wii and PS3 predicted the future of gaming – did they get it right?
records.summary: Both launched in 2006, with contrasting visions of gaming – one focused on accessibility, the other on technical ambition – each leaving a lasting legacy • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here The main focus of the games industry this week is, of course, the release of Grand Theft Auto VI – a game that could define the next decade for the industry. For this week’s newsletter though, I wanted to direct your attention two decades into the past. In November 2006, two console manufacturers launched their competing – and wildly different – visions of what the future of video games would look like. Twenty years later, it’s clear that somehow they were both right. And yet, in some ways, they were both wrong. For Nintendo, the Wii was the natural extension of its famous maxim, Kareta Gijutsu no Suihei Shikō – roughly translated as lateral thinking with withered technology. Coined by the company’s legendary engineer Gunpei Yokoi, father of the Game Boy, the phrase described a philosophy in which old tech could be combined with smart ideas to provide amazing new gaming possibilities. The Game Boy itself used a slow, old Sharp LR35902 processor and a sickly green monochrome screen, but it also came with Tetris and worked for ages on four AA batteries. With sales of 65m, it was vastly more successful than hi-tech rivals such as the Atari Lynx and Sega Game Gear.

records.title: NI Water Works - Cornagrade Road Enniskillen 3 Aug
records.summary: Essential Water Infrastructure Improvement Work gets underway – Cornagrade Road, Enniskillen NI Water is set to commence an upgrade of the water infrastructure on Cornagrade Road, Enniskillen in early August for approximately 6 weeks. The work will see around 400m of new watermain being laid along Cornagrade Road, starting at Cherrymount Roundabout on Monday 3 rd August and progressing as far as the second entrance to Kilmacormick Road. To facilitate the laying of this new watermain, a lane closure will be in place around each working area and signage will be in place. Working areas will be kept as short as possible (around 100m) with temporary traffic lights in place to manage the flow of traffic. Access to residential and business properties on and adjacent to Cornagrade Road will be available at all times, although parking spaces within the working area will be affected for a short period of time while the pipelaying passes. Any bus stop located within a working area will be temporarily relocated.

records.title: Derry - NIW Scheme - Racecourse Rd - from 27 July
records.summary: Essential water network upgrade to get underway on Racecourse Road, Ballyarnett NI Water is set to begin an essential watermain upgrade on Racecourse Road, Ballyarnett (Derry/Londonderry) on Monday 27 th July to improve the resilience of the local water supply network. The work, which involves laying around 170 metres of new watermain between Carnhill Roundabout and Greenhaw Road, will replace a section of the 50-year-old Ballyarnett Water Trunkmain which has been prone to bursts. The upgrade will help to protect homes from flooding, should a burst occur in the future, and provide improved access for NI Water maintenance. A l ane closure controlled by temporary traffic lights will be in place on Racecourse Road around the working area from Monday 27 th July for four weeks. A further two weeks of work will take place in the adjacent verge which will not require any traffic management. Temporary traffic lights will be manned during peak hours and access to properties will be maintained at all times, although parking spaces within the working area will be temporarily unavailable.
